answer: Record the 1839 Hollow Farm barn and the building now standing at Combe Farm as two distinct E24 Physical Human-Made Thing instances linked by an E81 Transformation, not as one object that simply moved. E81's scope note names 'reconstructions ... of historical buildings' as a characteristic case, and E24's own scope note addresses this exact threshold: a product that reuses 'larger parts or most of the original matter and structure' still gets 'a new, distinct identity' once the intervention is obvious and sufficient, with the material continuity captured by also documenting the event as E81. E11 Modification's scope note draws the same boundary from the other side: when destruction of the old and production of the new 'using parts or material from the originals' co-occur, 'the new items have separate identities' and E81 applies instead of mere Modification. Here the move plus the ~70% frame reuse, the whole rotted bay replaced, and the new roof covering and plinth walls push the case over that line -- this is not conservation/repair of one continuing object. A 2015 mailing-list exchange on exactly this scenario (moving/rebuilding immobile buildings) corroborates the reading: Martin Doerr argued the SIG should treat any such re-erection as new construction 'regardles how much simiarity and old substance it carries' because it requires new foundations and breaks the building's natural boundary with the ground (thread t0821) -- though that thread records no formal SIG vote, so it is his argued position, not a ratified rule; the officially adopted E81/E24/E11 scope notes are the primary basis here. Suggested structure: Hollow Farm barn (E24) --P124 transformed <-- [E81 Transformation, 1938] --P123 resulted in--> Combe Farm barn (E24). The 1839 tithe survey documents the former instance; the estate plaque is evidence asserting the latter's derivation from the former, not proof they are the same instance.
